procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 17, 1964 of the Madras High Court in Appeal Suit No. 375 of 1961.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Subordinate Judge dismissed the respondent's (plaintiff's) suit (Original Suit No. 30 of 1959) for specific performance. The High Court reversed the decision of the Trial Court and decreed the claim of the respondent for specific performance.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appellants 1 & 2 appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's decree, and restored the Trial Court's decree (Wanchoo and Shah, JJ., Bachawat, J. dissenting).

directions: The decree passed by the High Court is set aside.
The decree passed by the trial court restored.
There will be no order as to costs in this Court and in the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether a plaintiff in a suit for specific performance must plead and prove that he was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract continuously from the date of the contract until the hearing of the suit.

facts: The Trial Court made a specific finding that the plaintiff (respondent) was 'at no time ready and willing to perform his part of the contract' and dismissed the suit for specific performance on this ground.
On appeal, the High Court granted a decree for specific performance in favor of the plaintiff.
The High Court did not consider, challenge, or overturn the Trial Court's finding regarding the plaintiff's lack of readiness and willingness.
law: In a suit for specific performance, the plaintiff must plead and prove a continuous readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract from the date of the contract to the time of the hearing.
Failure by the plaintiff to prove this continuous readiness and willingness will result in the dismissal of their suit.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court could only grant a decree for specific performance if it was satisfied that the plaintiff was continuously ready and willing to perform his contractual obligations.
The Court found that the High Court had erred by granting the decree without addressing and setting aside the Trial Court's explicit finding that the plaintiff was *not* ready and willing.
The burden was on the plaintiff to establish this fact, and the Trial Court had found that he failed to do so. This finding was a key ground for the dismissal of the suit at the trial level.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the Trial Court's finding and held that because the plaintiff had failed to prove he was continuously ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, a decree for specific performance could not be granted and his suit must fail.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court could grant a decree for specific performance without considering and setting aside the trial court's finding that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.

facts: The Trial Court dismissed the plaintiff's (respondent's) suit for specific performance.
A key finding by the Trial Court was that the plaintiff was at no time ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
The plaintiff appealed to the High Court, which reversed the Trial Court's decision and granted a decree for specific performance.
In the High Court, the plaintiff did not challenge the Trial Court's finding regarding his lack of readiness and willingness.
The High Court's judgment did not consider, discuss, or set aside this specific finding of the Trial Court.
law: In a suit for specific performance, the plaintiff must plead and prove that he was continuously ready and willing to perform his part of the contract from the date of the contract until the date of the hearing.
If a plaintiff fails to prove this continuous readiness and willingness, his suit for specific performance is liable to fail.
application: The Supreme Court established that the plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform the contract was a vital issue that had to be proven for a decree of specific performance to be granted.
The Court noted that the Trial Court had made an express finding that the plaintiff was *not* ready and willing, and this was one of the grounds for dismissing the suit.

The Supreme Court found it was a critical error for the High Court to grant a decree for specific performance without first considering and setting aside the Trial Court's adverse finding on this essential issue.

Since the Trial Court's finding was based on evidence, was not challenged by the plaintiff in the High Court, and was not held to be incorrect by the High Court, the Supreme Court determined that this finding must be accepted.
Accepting the Trial Court's finding meant that the plaintiff had failed to prove a necessary condition for his claim.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court could not grant a decree for specific performance because it had failed to address and overturn the Trial Court's finding that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. Since this is a mandatory requirement for such a decree, and the Trial Court's finding stood unchallenged, the plaintiff's claim for specific performance had to fail.

issue.issue_text: Whether the suit for specific performance was barred by delay.

facts: The High Court had previously considered the issue of delay and rejected the contention that it barred the suit for specific performance.
The High Court found that the delay between April 30, 1959, and July 30, 1959, was not undue and did not constitute abandonment or waiver of the contract.
When the case came before the Supreme Court, the appellants (the party who would benefit from a finding of delay) chose not to argue this point any further.
application: The text explicitly states, "The appellants no longer urge that the respondent was disentitled to relief on the ground of delay."
Because the appellants abandoned this argument on appeal, the Supreme Court did not need to rule on the merits of whether the delay was a bar to the suit.
The High Court's decision on this specific point was therefore left unchallenged by the appellants at the Supreme Court level.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the suit was barred by delay because the appellants did not press the issue on appeal, effectively accepting the High Court's prior ruling that the delay was not a bar to relief.

issue.issue_text: Whether time was of the essence of the contract.

facts: The trial court had found that time was of the essence based on three circumstances: (1) the written agreements fixed specific dates for performance, (2) the agreements included default/penalty clauses, and (3) the sellers were in urgent need of money.
The agreements in question did not contain an explicit clause stating in unmistakable language that time was to be of the essence.
law: For contracts involving the sale of immovable property, it is normally presumed that time is not of the essence.

To make time of the essence, the parties' intention must be shown through either (a) express stipulations in unmistakable language, or (b) surrounding circumstances that are sufficiently strong to displace the normal presumption.
Merely fixing a period for performance or including a default/penalty clause does not, by itself, make time of the essence of the contract.
application: The Supreme Court found that there was no express stipulation in the agreements making time of the essence.
The Court then evaluated the circumstances and found them insufficient to displace the presumption.
The Court reasoned that the fixation of a date for performance and the existence of a default clause were not, on their own, enough to prove that time was essential.

Regarding the sellers' urgent need for money, the Court noted that they had already received a partial payment of Rs. 3006/-, which presumably provided temporary relief, and there was no evidence they sought other funds when the deal was delayed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that time was not of the essence of the contract because there was no express stipulation to that effect, and the surrounding circumstances were not strong enough to overcome the ordinary presumption that time is not essential in contracts for the sale of land.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a plaintiff in a suit for specific performance must plead and prove that he was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract continuously from the date of the contract until the hearing of the suit.
appellant_arguments: The respondent was not ready and willing to get the sale deed executed.
The respondent deliberately delayed paying the balance of the consideration and performing the agreement.
The respondent admitted in cross-examination that on a specific date (April 30, 1959), he was not ready to purchase the stamp paper or take the sale deed.
respondent_arguments: The respondent pleaded that he was always ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
The execution of the sale deed was postponed at the request of the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court could grant a decree for specific performance without considering and setting aside the trial court's finding that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not have granted the decree without overturning the trial court's finding that the respondent was not ready and willing, a finding which the appellants argued was correct.
respondent_arguments: The High Court rightly decreed the suit for specific performance, implying its decision was correct despite the trial court's finding.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the suit for specific performance was barred by delay.
appellant_arguments: The respondent was deliberately putting off payment and delaying performance, and the reasons he gave for the delay were found to be 'obviously untrue' by the trial court.
respondent_arguments: Any delay was not his fault, but occurred at the request of the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether time was of the essence of the contract.
appellant_arguments: Timely performance was crucial as the appellants were 'badly in need of money', and the respondent had defaulted on the stipulated timeline.
respondent_arguments: Time was not of the essence, as the appellants themselves requested the postponement of the sale deed's execution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Unexplained delay on the part of a party seeking specific performance of a contract is a valid ground for a court to refuse such relief.
obiter: The special jurisdiction of equity is to disregard the letter of the contract in ascertaining what the parties to the contract are to be taken as having really intended.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's core finding was that the High Court committed a legal error by granting a decree for specific performance without first considering and reversing the trial court's explicit finding of fact that the plaintiff (respondent) was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. The failure to prove continuous readiness and willingness is fatal to a suit for specific performance.
legal_tests_applied: A plaintiff in a suit for specific performance must plead and prove that he was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract continuously between the date of the contract and the date of hearing of the suit.

An appellate court can only grant a decree for specific performance contrary to the trial court's findings if it first reverses the trial court's finding that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform the contract.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the suit was barred by delay was rejected, with the court affirming the High Court's finding that 'neither the delay nor the failure to explain the delay was a ground for refusing relief.'

The appellant's argument that time was of the essence of the contract was rejected based on the principle that a court of equity will grant specific performance even if 'the contract has not been literally performed by the plaintiff as regards the time limit specified.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that mere delay did not disentitle him to relief was accepted, as the court held that 'the High Court rightly found that neither the delay nor the failure to explain the delay was a ground for refusing relief.'

The respondent's position that time was not of the essence was implicitly accepted through the court's citation of the equitable principle that performance will be enjoined even if a specified time limit has not been literally met.
policy_considerations: An appellate court cannot ignore a crucial finding of fact made by the trial court. To grant a decree for specific performance, the High Court was required to first reverse the trial court's finding that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform the contract. Failing to do so undermines the judicial process and the role of the trial court as the primary finder of fact.
